data.title: NVIDIA, Caterpillar & Nike: Three Corporate Events That Could Move Markets
data.description:
• Market volatility rose following the midterms, putting the AI trade and data center buildout under renewed scrutiny
  • NVIDIA, Caterpillar, and Nike headline next week’s corporate events, offering important clues on AI investment, construction demand, and the consumer
  • Procter & Gamble’s Investor Day may add further consumer color, with easing energy costs and a bit better labor market potentially supporting the 2027 outlook

If you’re hyper-focused on markets and geopolitics, it feels like the world has changed in the past week-plus. The U.S. midterm elections brought about a surprising volatility thrust, first with a premature “clearing event” rally on Wednesday, November 4, followed by 2026’s broadest-based selloff on Thursday. The plunge was the Nasdaq 100’s biggest since March 2020. The bulls were back in town to kick off this week, though, and all 11 S&P 500® sectors posted Monday gains.

AI on Thin Ice?

Macro storylines have no doubt been rewritten. The AI trade and data center buildout are being called into question ahead of the new, much bluer Congress set to take the reins on Capitol Hill in January. It remains to be seen how throttled AI investment will be in 2027 and beyond, but even before voters cast ballots, price action in data center plays was dismal.

Many chip stocks, shares of data center infrastructure names, and power providers were down 40% or more from their respective 52-week highs. Now, all eyes are on late-season reporters, but more importantly, on what company executives have to say about the megatrend’s future.

NVIDIA’s Busy Calendar Amid Drama at the Top

The elephant in the room is NVIDIA (NVDA) and CEO Jensen Huang. The so-called “Godfather of AI” has laid low following the news of his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. After a 4% decline on Monday, the world’s second-most valuable company is 25% off its early-October record high.

NVIDIA’s corporate event calendar remains loaded, with speaking engagements slated early next week at Supercomputing SC 2026, starting Sunday; Microsoft Ignite 2026, beginning Tuesday; and the TomorrowX Summit 2026, kicking off on the 17th as well.

The chip designer and cornerstone of the AI buildout then reports fiscal Q3 2027 earnings that afternoon, presumably with Jensen offering commentary thereafter. No shortage of drama there.

CAT, NKE, and PG Offer Mid-Quarter Updates

But beyond NVIDIA and Wall Street’s version of supermarket tabloids, there’s real corporate commentary on deck. Our team highlights three companies that each provide a unique lens on the macro backdrop for global portfolio managers and traders alike to weigh:

November 17: Caterpillar Bernstein Fireside Chat

Tuesday next week will be a thriller. Along with NVIDIA’s series of events, arguably the most critical AI-related player in the Industrials sector sits down with Chad Dillard of Bernstein to discuss the latest trends in construction.

Recall that last week’s October jobs report revealed a surprising uptick in manufacturing employment. But will the AI-buildout boom live on in the wake of the blue tsunami? And how is global construction demand trending beyond just tech and AI? These are some of the questions the Street hopes to have answered.

For shareholders, CAT has been a catastrophe since notching an all-time high at the end of the first half. Now in a more than 40% drawdown, value investors are curious, while growth investors may be left holding the bag. Still, the Texas-based company and second-largest Dow component reported a 17% jump in Q3 sales last month, driven by high demand in its Power & Energy segments.

But shares tumbled on rising inventories, casting a black cloud over what was already a darkening price-action backdrop. We’ll see if Tuesday’s fireside chat relieves AI anxiety.

November 17: Nike Investor Day

Yes, times are uncertain about anything related to data centers, but consumers may feel like the macro tides are turning in their favor. Another result of the big Democratic victory was the increased likelihood of de-escalation in the Middle East.

While nobody knows if the war in Iran is on its last legs, the oil market seems to think normalization is not far away. Brent crude oil was above $115 in late October, and it’s now near $90. Gasoline futures, meanwhile, point to $3.60 at the pump, perhaps by Thanksgiving. Along with a decent employment backdrop, there’s some reason for cheer ahead of the holiday shopping season.

For Nike (NKE) and other Consumer Discretionary companies, they’ll take all the macro help they can get. Down 37% year-to-date (and the worst Dow stock in 2026), the footwear stalwart hopes to assuage investors’ fears both at its Analyst Day on Tuesday and with fiscal Q2 2027 results due out a month later. CEO Elliott Hill has his hands full figuring out today’s market structure.

Be on the lookout for strategy details at next week’s event, and don’t overlook the stock’s very high 8.6% short interest.

November 19: Procter & Gamble Investor Day

The consumer is also in focus on Thursday next week. Blue-chip Procter & Gamble (PG) welcomes analysts and shareholders at its Investor Day a week before Turkey Day. The Consumer Staples stock has been on a heater, rallying from $143 in early October (when tech peaked) to a record high of $170 in recent days. That’s an unusual bullish burst for this typically low-volatility safety play. Now sporting a P/E multiple north of 24x, shares might feel a bit rich.

Still, PG is only barely above its February high. Tariff headwinds are now largely over, and hope on the energy-cost horizon could help boost the bottom line in CY 2027. The webcast begins at 2 p.m. ET, with President and CEO Shailesh Jejurikar, among others, commenting on the company’s long-term strategy and value creation for shareholders.

The Bottom Line

Earnings season may be winding down, but investors aren’t cheated by the corporate event risk calendar. NVIDIA will be in the spotlight, while Caterpillar might brief the Street on what the future looks like for data center buildout demand. All the while, the consumer story appears more sanguine amid oil’s plunge and a sturdy labor market backdrop. As bulls and bears play a little tug-of-war, key clues may emerge at these upcoming events.

data.title: Mid-Q4 Investor Conferences Update: After AI Selloff, Wall Street Searches for Answers
data.description:
• The Nasdaq 100 shed 7% in October as investors rotated into defensive and real-economy sectors, with Health Care at record highs and Consumer Staples posting their best month since 2000
  • With Q3 numbers in hand, conference commentary is the next catalyst: CEOs have just weeks to set the tone before sell-side 2027 outlooks, with Microsoft Ignite, NVIDIA earnings, and Anthropic’s IPO all ahead
  • Capex trends and consumer health are the key themes to watch, as hyperscaler debt financing could pressure rates and negative real income trends raise the risk of a holiday spending pullback

The AI trade came under attack in October. The Nasdaq 100 shed 7% as investors flocked to real-economy stocks and defensive sectors. Health Care notched record highs, while Consumer Staples put up their best monthly return since 2000. The bond market had its say as Q4 got going, too. Credit default swap spreads were constantly quoted in the financial press, even before outright post-earnings crashes in stocks like Alphabet (GOOGL) and Intel (INTC).

Explain Yourselves

Q3 numbers are in hand. Now, it’s all about the commentary and path forward. That’s what makes the upcoming conference stretch so crucial. CEOs have just weeks to properly set the tone before the sell side litters the street with its 2027 outlooks. Meanwhile, many volatility catalysts lie directly ahead. Even beyond the midterms, tech investors look forward to Microsoft Ignite, NVIDIA earnings, and Anthropic’s IPO, potentially before Thanksgiving.

Curious Cross-Asset Connections

Are AI stocks at risk of further declines? That’s the big question asset allocators ponder. Perhaps good news can be gleaned from the bond market. Globally, borrowing costs have eased after governing part of the data center buildout theme in October. But the hyperscalers continue their debt-financing binge, leaving the door open to another leg higher in the rates markets. As analysts, investors, and executives gather around the world, clues on capex trends will not only be closely monitored but will potentially drive markets as we put the bow on 2026.

Still Strong Spending, Eyes on the Holidays

And then there’s the consumer, who collectively faces a higher cost of living and wage gains that simply don’t keep up with inflation. Indications are that gas prices are dipping, but at a seemingly snail’s pace. True, it has been foolish to doubt the power of household spending, but the longer negative real income trends persist, the greater the chance of a more protracted purse-string pullback. Consumer company and bank leaders’ commentary at investor conferences will be particularly revealing ahead of the holidays.

data.title: Tracking the AI Buildout
data.description:
This isn’t our first bubble. In fact, we have invested through many bubbles from dotcom, energy trading, China (2x), commodities, housing, mobile, fracking, cloud, marijuana, and now AI. Each was different in its trajectory, speed, size, inflation, and deflation.

Some bubbles are big but narrowly focused (dotcom), some are gradual that have systematic ramifications (housing), and some grow and pop with limited economic consequences (marijuana).

This AI one is already REALLY BIG and PERVASIVE; so big that its path will likely be the dominant factor in driving equity and bond markets plus the global economy in the coming years. 

The AI infrastructure buildout has some pretty mind-blowing numbers behind it. Based on current forecasts, this is bigger than any of the big infrastructure spends over the past few hundred years. Measuring the spend vs the size of the economy, the only past infrastructure spend that comes close was the railway expansion back in the late 1800s. We will see, as the railway buildout lasted two decades and the AI infrastructure spend is only a few years old now.

A very important caveat for the above chart, which certainly encourages enthusiasm for this bubble, is the path of investment returns. The railway bubble lasted 20 years but railway investors enjoyed strong returns in the 1870s and very poor results in the 1880s even as the infrastructure spend and buildout persisted. Same with the internet; 2000 to 2003 was abysmal for stocks but cable continued to be laid. For a sports analogy, you don’t want to stick around till the end of the game, in fact you may want to leave at halftime. Our guess (given expectations are high and still rising, while company sizes are already massive), we are in the first half of the buildout but the stock market may be at the second hydration break.

The AI infrastructure buildout is real, with lots of capital and little concern over rising costs as leadership or ‘being there’ is paramount. And it is not just the mega data centre projects, as we may all have a DGX Spark in our garage in a few years. Will there be a positive ROI (return on investment) for all this infrastructure? Perhaps —the demand continues to build as do the use cases. Add shortages or tight supply of memory, chips, power tie-ins, or simply a shortage of compute, and the enthusiasm is easy to justify. Conversely, some have already modelled that the global economy may have to spend more on AI compute than food to justify what is forecast to be built out. Or the labs will make more compute efficiency gains. Open models vs closed, integrated customer solutions vs stand-alone offerings. Sticking with our game analogy, there are a lot of twists and turns ahead.

Regardless of your views on the next leg of this bubble and the market/economic implications, you are exposed. This is an everywhere bubble, evident in chips, memory, optics, storage and LLM providers. Now it has spread to lift shares in many industrials involved in building or power to even boring utilities. Or from a geographic perspective, pick an equity market and there is often a good amount of AI exposure. The U.S. equity market leads this, thanks to many of the megacaps and model providers. The top 10 weighted names in the S&P 500, totaling over 40% of the index, are all AI plays. Emerging markets and Japan have a lot of exposure on the tech hardware side, including memory and chips.

Even if you have limited AI exposure on the equity side of the portfolio, you may be getting some on the bond side. The investment grade fixed-income universe in the U.S. used to be about 7-8% weighted to the megacap AI names and providers of the picks and shovels or chips and connectivity. That weight started to rise a year ago and now sits at 12.1%. The biggest increases came from Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, SpaceX and Oracle.

Even if you don’t own many direct AI-related bonds or many direct AI-related equities, you are still exposed. This rapid bond issuance is one of the contributors to rising bond yields everywhere. Yes, this is such a big deal it is influencing government bond yields because of competition for capital. And the capex spending, much of it devoted to building data centers to drive AI compute and training, is helping supercharge economic growth.

There is no easy way to accurately measure this economic impact, but it is noticeable. We isolated two sub-components of U.S. GDP that would be largely impacted by the data centre spend, namely fixed investment in information processing and intellectual property spending. Over the past 30 years, these two have averaged about a +0.4% contribution to real GDP but currently are running at almost 1.0%. With AI-related capex accelerating in 2025 and in 2026, the impact is becoming very noticeable even in the headline GDP numbers.

For some context, this capex tech spending did spike in 2021 as remote or hybrid work required infrastructure spending. That was short lived. This tech spending was also big in late 1990s and that lasted for 3-4 years as the internet was built. Without this spending, the U.S. economy would certainly be growing at a slower pace. If it were to slow or even normalize, headline growth would take a hit. And this may cause other areas of economic weakness to become more apparent, such as struggling housing or the bifurcated consumer.

And if you don’t own many AI-related stocks or bonds or exposure to U.S. economy, you are still exposed. A good portion of this capex is spent on imports, which is helping economic growth in many other countries around the world.

AI has become a dominant factor in many equity markets around the world, and now it is driving bond yields plus boosting economic growth. AI is everywhere and everything.

Within our portfolios we have AI exposure, at a level we believe as reasonable. The technology is awesome and use cases continue to expand. It is a bubble, though fortunately we appear to still be in the ‘inflation’ stage. Given AI’s heft, there will likely be a number of oscillations in AI excitement, leading to oscillations in the market. This could persist for many quarters or even years, which brings us to how to watch for signs the bubble is at risk. We are not overly confident as history teaches us it will likely be something that surprises us all, but we do have a number of things we are focused on:

Earnings & expectations – The dotcom bubble didn’t end because pets.com launched, it just coincided with it. With hindsight, it was really that expectations grew so high that when the numbers, which were still growing nicely, couldn’t keep up with the hype, the market caps became unsustainable. For now, though, earnings have continued to deliver.

Economy & yields – This kind of spending is not overly sensitive to higher costs of capital, aka higher yields. But these higher yields are taking a toll on the overall economy. Should this drag begin to overwhelm the growth impulse from the capex spend, a cooling economy could easily start bubble deflation.

Decelerating growth – Markets react much more to the second derivative: changes in acceleration vs growth. Hyperscaler capex was $365B in 2025, more than doubling to $762B in 2026 based on reported and forecasts. 2027 forecasts are for continued growth to $1,125B but that implies the growth pace falling from 108% to 47%. Of course, forecasts can change but that could easily cause bubble deflation. Even though things are growing, the rate of change matters a lot.

CAPEX GROWS

Capital access – With the bond market being tapped from many issuers, higher yields being required is a sign of investor sceptics.  Keep an eye on credit default swaps (CDS) for big AI-related issuers.  There is now CDSs for Alphabet, which didn’t used to exist, while Oracle has theirs priced at 2.7%. The equity market’s ability to absorb future mega IPOs will also be a sign. So far so good though.

Final thoughts

This is a bubble that is big enough and pervasive enough that it will impact markets and economy. We are all in it now and we believe the key to navigating it will be to monitor its path. Be aware of your exposures, be opportunistic and be prudent by ensuring your portfolio has adequate diversification offsets.

This report is authored by CraigBasinger, Chief Market Strategist at Purpose Investments Inc.

Source: Charts are sourced to Bloomberg L.P., Purpose Investments Inc., and Richardson Wealth unless otherwise noted.

data.title: 4 Stocks to Watch This Earnings Season (Beyond Big Tech and AI)
data.description:
• AI jitters and rising rates are fueling a market rotation into once beaten-down defensive and real-economy stocks
  • Steel Dynamics, Nucor, Kroger, and Kimberly-Clark face key earnings reports and corporate catalysts in the days ahead
  • Earnings commentary, AI infrastructure demand, dealmaking developments, and even midterm election outcomes could determine whether the rotation has staying power

October has already provided a scare for tech investors. Information Technology was the lone S&P 500 sector in the red month-to-date coming into Friday, the 16th. AI jitters, rising interest rates, concerning CDS spreads, and even regulatory worries cooled the once red-hot megatrend.  

Will recent price action prove to be yet another buyable pullback? Or is something more sinister at play? Chances are, we’ll find out much more over the coming weeks as Q3 reports roll in. 

Healthy Rotation, Or a Messy Q4 Equity Backdrop?

For now, momentum traders find themselves strolling down unusual aisles. Indeed, as I.T. lags, defensive and rate-sensitive spaces such as Consumer Staples, Utilities, Health Care, and Materials have caught bids. Simply scan through price charts of blue chips in these real-economy sectors, and you’ll come across many apparent bottoming patterns. 

Now, normally, the bulls don’t want to see the safest parts of the global stock market outperforming risk-on areas. Historically, when defensives lead within a choppy tape, the chances increase that a durable bear market may be lurking around the corner. 

Today, though, it could simply be one big rotation, a move out of high-growth AI stocks and into equities that were beaten down too much by the sharp interest rate climb from late August through the early days of October. After all, they say rotation is the lifeblood of bull markets. We’ll see how it all shakes out. No matter the consequences, Q4 will probably continue to provide many compelling storylines. 

Narratives may take more twists and turns in the following sessions, too. Zooming in on a pair of the aforementioned non-tech sectors, several stocks could see unusual volatility that traders should keep on their radar. And while they don’t drip AI, recent company announcements show that data centers, large language models, and agentic programs have long tentacles that reach far beyond Silicon Valley. 

Steel Dynamics & Nucor: Bearish Q3 Preliminaries

First up: Steel Dynamics (STLD). The $35 billion market cap Materials sector company reports Q3 results after the bell on Monday, October 19. The Indiana-based cyclical firm has seen its stock surge 65% in the past year, boosted by big nationwide construction spending spurred by what else? Data centers.  

But it and industry peer Nucor (NUE) hit the skids in mid-September following soft preliminary earnings numbers. STLD executives said they expected third-quarter earnings of $5.34–$5.38 per share, far shy of consensus estimates at the time. Compared to a year ago, however, even the low-end number would represent a near-doubling of operating EPS. 

Managing Expectations

Could the bar be low enough for STLD to hurdle with flying colors? It remains to be seen, but the stock has paced itself for the better part of six months. After peaking at $289 in mid-June, STLD has flirted with its 200-day moving average since the middle of the year after a smelter-hot rally that began in August 2025 at $120. A new CEO is at the helm, and trade policy matters greatly for this steel company. Monday’s report and earnings call will be of particular interest. 

As for Nucor, the $58 billion Materials company’s shares have enjoyed (and then weathered) similar price developments. Its Q3 report is confirmed for Monday, October 26, BMO. The North Carolina-based name announced a $105 million expansion of its Indiana utility towers facility to add capacity to manufacture poles and other products to support power transmission and distribution infrastructure. A healthier grid is critical to the AI buildout. Comments from management will be particularly practical in light of recent AI news. 

Kroger: Contentious Investor Day, Amid Soft Sales, Rising Costs, and a Botched Merger

Next, Kroger (KR) has their cart full in the days ahead. The country’s largest stand-alone retail grocer comes through the earnings checkout line in early December. In the here and now, it hosts an Investor Day on Tuesday, October 20. Just recently, on October 12, the Consumer Staples player announced it would eliminate 3,000 corporate jobs (37% of its ~8,200 corporate workforce) as part of a three-year restructuring.1 

The headcount cut is an AI-efficiency byproduct. Cost-conscious consumers pressure its net sales, while record-high diesel prices surely drive up the expense side of the ledger as the holiday season approaches. 

Shares are down 9% over the past 12 months, though KR has rallied since the start of the second half. Investors will seek answers on Tuesday regarding the saga between the company and rival Albertsons Companies (ACI). Reported last week, Albertsons asked a Delaware court to force Kroger to pay as much as $9.3 billion over the dissolved $24.6 billion merger between the two industry stalwarts. That nixed deal has been an overhang for years, potentially making the Investor Day a little spicier. 

Kimberly-Clark: Executives Appear Sanguine Ahead of a Potential Kenvue Integration

Finally, Kimberly-Clark Corporation (KMB) issued a bullish preliminary earnings statement on Thursday, October 15, ahead of full Q3 results confirmed for Thursday, November 5, BMO. The often-quiet Consumer Staples stock surged nearly 5%, almost its best day since April 2024.  

Shareholders needed the boost, as KMB was down 18% YoY beforehand. Specifically, KMB now expects to earn an adjusted profit of $1.70 per share, about $0.11 above estimates, with net sales of $4.134 billion (down 0.4% from a year ago but above forecasts). 

KMB has M&A on its mind as well. The $33 billion market cap company received conditional approval from the European Commission on October 13, for its $40 billion (or $48.7 billion including debt) acquisition of Kenvue (KVUE). Paired with the upbeat earnings pre-announcement, it could be a successful end to the year, assuming the deal is finalized in the coming months. 

The Bottom Line

Plenty of story-stocks and recent alpha generators are outside AI glamor companies. Absolute and relative strength have ticked up in real-economy sectors that were beaten up as investor dollars flowed to tech. Macro conditions, such as ebbing Treasury rates and the upcoming U.S. midterm elections, are wildcards. Still, traders and portfolio managers should listen up for commentary in perhaps unusual places this earnings season.

data.title: ETF Survival of the Fittest: Record Launches Meet Accelerating Delistings
data.description:
• The US ETF market is pacing toward a historic launch record in 2026, driven by 1,023 new product debuts in the first eight months alone (52% YoY growth), alongside near-record inflows
  • With 169 ETF delistings logged through the first three quarters and Q4 historically serving as the peak period for fund liquidations, 2026 is on track to potentially mark the highest annual closure volume since 2018
  • Rather than signalling weakness, rising delistings reflect a hyper-efficient marketplace where issuers rapidly retire underperforming or low-liquidity strategies to reallocate resources toward proven investor demand

The exchange-traded fund (ETF) market is pacing toward a record-breaking year in 2026, driven by an unprecedented wave of new product launches and historic capital inflows. In the first eight months of 2026 alone, 1,023 new ETFs debuted on major exchanges (a 52% jump from the same period last year), while total year-to-date inflows are on the verge of clearing an annual record at $1.47 trillion.1 

Coming on top of the banner record set in 2025, this relentless expansion underscores how deeply embedded ETFs have become across both retail and institutional portfolios.

The driver behind this sustained appetite lies in ETF’s unmatched flexibility, liquidity, and tax efficiency compared to traditional investment vehicles. Active ETFs have seen particularly explosive growth, capturing a massive share of new allocations as traditional asset managers continue converting mutual fund strategies into ETF structures. While passive, index-tracking funds still form the core foundation of long-term portfolios, active ETFs give managers room to navigate volatile macro environments, implement option-overlay income strategies, and offer targeted thematic exposure.

This rapid shift toward active management has spurred a continuous cycle of product innovation, and with it, a faster rate of product turnover.

ETF Attrition Accelerates: What’s Behind the Delisting Surge?

Parallel to the historic launch pace, ETF delistings are mounting quickly. According to Wall Street Horizon data, the current tally for 2026 ETF delistings has already reached 169 through the first three quarters (data as of September 21, 2026). This compares to 188 closures in 2025, 169 in 2024, and 214 in 2023. Historically, the fourth quarter stands as the most active period for fund liquidations, as asset managers routinely clean up balance sheets, rationalize product lines, and optimize tax-loss harvesting profiles prior to year-end. With Q4 still ahead, 2026 is on track to potentially become the highest annual delisting period in Wall Street Horizon’s dataset dating back to 2018.

What is driving this elevated delisting activity? It is primarily a function of the sheer volume of product launches seen over recent years, coupled with structural shifts in issuer behavior, evolving macro conditions, and shrinking tolerance for underperforming funds. With hundreds of niche and thematic funds hitting the market annually, issuers are running aggressive product experiments. If a strategy fails to gather meaningful AUM or establish trading liquidity within 12 to 24 months, providers are increasingly swift to pull the plug rather than subsidize non-viable funds.

Rather than viewing these elevated delisting numbers as a sign of industry distress, analysts increasingly interpret them as evidence of a hyper-efficient marketplace. The modern ETF ecosystem operates with a high degree of darwinism: capital moves rapidly to winning strategies, while unsuccessful products are systematically cut to make way for new ideas.

The Bottom Line

The record setting 2026 ETF landscape highlights a market defined by both rapid expansion and constant refinement. As asset managers roll out record numbers of active and specialized products to capture historic inflows, the margin for underperforming funds has narrowed significantly. The rising tide of delistings reflects an industry that is both highly competitive and structural in its discipline, quickly retiring stagnant strategies to make room for market-driven innovation. For custodians, data providers, and back-office teams, tracking this accelerating product lifecycle, from launch to final payout, remains imperative.

data.title: Real-Economy Corporate Events Investors Should Watch This Month
data.description:
• AI drama and jumpy Treasury yields pressure tech stocks with the Fed in play within a macro-focused tape
  • Salesforce, FedEx, General Mills, McDonald’s, Darden Restaurants, and Sherwin-Williams are company-level stories worth watching
  • Corporate presentations and shareholder meetings could offer fresh clues on consumer, industrial, and business trends

Never a dull moment in the AI trade. Over the weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged the industry to tap the brakes on AI frontier development. The tech leader’s blog post made the rounds ahead of Fed Week and as geopolitical tensions escalated in the Middle East.  

Rival CEO Sam Altman at OpenAI backed Amodei, with SpaceX (SPCX) chief Elon Musk jumping on the cool-it bandwagon. President Trump then spoke out against the proposed slowdown, asserting that the U.S. must continue to lead the way in AI. 

The AI Trade Feels the Heat

These high-profile theatrics left a mark on early-week trading. The Nasdaq 100 ETF (QQQ) briefly dipped to a seven-week low, while the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) sunk further toward its late-July nadir before dip-buyers stepped up. 

Tech storylines and AI intrigue are perhaps, unsurprisingly, the prominent narratives, along with drama in the bond market. There’s a lack of single-stock volatility catalysts now that earnings season is in the books. The conference calendar is also less packed, though plenty of major gatherings wait in the wings. 

Corporate America (Beyond AI Leaders) Have Their Say

What is not in short supply? Analyst Days, Business Updates, and Shareholder Meetings. This is a key stretch for companies to get ahead of all the sell-side year-ahead outlooks, and CEOs and CFOs often like to set the tone before the Street puts proverbial pen to paper. Our team noticed a handful of consumer-related corporate confabs in the queue.  

While enterprise is en vogue with Salesforce’s (CRM) Dreamforce event during this options expiration week, household names like McDonald’s (MCD), Darden Restaurants (DRI), and General Mills (GIS) host analysts and/or stockholders before the books close on Q3. There are other notables, too, including Dow Inc. (DOW), Sherwin-Williams (SHW), and FedEx (FDX). 

Wednesday, September 16: Salesforce Dreamforce & Dow Fireside Chat

Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff and co serve up the latest software industry developments, with CNBC’s Jim Cramer on hand. The event wraps up on Thursday, as does the Morgan Stanley 14th Annual Laguna Conference 2026.  

Chemicals company Dow presents at that West Coast multi-industry gathering. Shares of the $21 billion market-cap Materials sector firm have been under pressure since peaking when the S&P 500 troughed in late March. Once a hot play among traders as the conflict in Iran first escalated, agriculture stocks have sunk amid softer fertilizer and related prices. In July, Dow posted a solid double beat on revenue and earnings, although a light guide kept buyers in check. We’ll hear the latest developments this week ahead of its October 22 Q3 report.

Tuesday, September 22: FedEx Dataworks Chief Speaks at HumanX Amsterdam 2026; Shareholder Meeting Monday, September 22

Next week, eyes turn to a slew of big names. FedEx is first up. Like the broader Industrials sector of the S&P 500, the Air Freight & Logistics industry firm has struggled, given much higher fuel prices, namely record-high diesel. Middle East tensions do the multinational corporation no favors, either. But streamlined operations following the FedEx Freight (FDFX) spin would seem to help its C-suite team with targeted execution.  

Expect to learn details when Vishal Talwar, Chief Digital & Information Officer & President of FedEx Dataworks, takes the podium at HumanX Amsterdam 2026 on Tuesday, the 22nd. After that, the shipper hosts its Annual General Meeting on the final Monday of the month. 

Wednesday, September 23: General Mills Q1 2027 Earnings Date; Analyst Day, Thursday, September 24

There’s nothing more down-home consumer than General Mills. Stung by GLP-1 adoption and perhaps in the crosshairs of the Secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, this Consumer Staples stock is down 25% from a year ago. Its management team recently reaffirmed FY 2027 guidance, which may have helped buoy the stock.  

Some Americans are slimming down on weight-loss medications, and GIS is getting leaner on its own, divesting assets to focus on its core competencies. General Mills has a lot to prove, though, namely its declining North American segment sales. Be on the lookout for potential volatility on September 23, with further color from the cereal maker at its September 24 AGM.

Wednesday, September 23: McDonald’s Investor Day & Darden Restaurants Shareholder Meeting (followed by Q1 2027 Earnings on Thursday)

Restaurants then snatch the spotlight. McDonald’s hosts its 2026 Investor Day a week before quarter-end, just as Olive Garden and Ruth’s Chris owner Darden Restaurants holds its shareholder meeting. Investors and market-watchers writ large could hear key consumer spending nuggets. 

The cost of living remains top of mind for families across the country, with less than seven weeks until the U.S. midterm elections. DRI stays in the news with its fiscal Q1 earnings report confirmed for Thursday, September 24.

Thursday, September 24: Sherwin-Williams Financial Community Presentation

Last to paint the tape is Sherwin-Williams. Pull up a 1-year performance chart, and yes, it’s like watching paint dry. In the middle of its range, precisely flat YTD, a depressed housing market and an abandoned acquisition earlier in 2026 have left SHW in no-man’s-land. 

Still, the $78 billion market-cap Materials sector stalwart put up an earnings triple play in July, beating on the top and bottom lines while lifting guidance. The stock climbed, but didn’t make much summer headway. Technicals aside, fundamental investors should get a look at the latest happenings at the Sherwin-Williams Financial Community Presentation on Thursday, September 24.

The Bottom Line

It feels like the market and economy hinge on the latest AI developments and breaking news out of the White House and Iran. Throw in spicy Treasury yields and a Fed that’s all-systems-go on rate hikes (it appears), and it’s easy to stray from non-tech companies and the stories they relay about the Main Street economy. Keep your eye out for updates on industry and consumer trends now through month-end, as they could reveal clues that the macroscope misses.

data.title: Dodging the September Slump: Inside the 2026 IPO Rebound
data.description:
• 2026 is pacing toward the strongest IPO performance since the 2021 boom, logging 331 new filings and 280 completed offerings YTD, already exceeding full Q1–Q3 levels from 2025
  • Only 10 companies have withdrawn their IPO applications so far in 2026, a drastic drop from the 157 capitulation withdrawals seen during the 2022 rate shock
  • Anthropic’s rumored timeline shift into October is a tactical move to bypass September’s historical seasonality, inflation prints, and Fed rate decision, setting up a potential green light for mega-cap peers like OpenAI to follow before year-end

There’s no debating that 2026 has been a stellar year thus far for IPO activity, with 331 new filings YTD (as of September 8). Following two years in the deep freeze and a tepid, watching-and-waiting recovery, Wall Street’s primary issuance desk is officially back in business.

But as the Q3 countdown clock winds into its final 20 days, a wall of headline worry threatens to spoil the party. With uncertainty looming around the escalation of the Iran war, persistent inflation, wild swings in oil prices, and rising tariff threats, is that tide about to turn? 

Syndicate desks got their first real test this week following reports that Anthropic is pushing its targeted mega-listing from late September into mid-October.1 On the surface, the headline gave market watchers a quick flash of anxiety. But under the hood, Dario Amodei and his underwriting syndicate (potentially led by Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs2) aren’t running scared, they’re possibly dodging a dense gauntlet of September catalysts during a month that is historically known for being brutal for stocks. 

Why launch a roadshow right over next week’s Fed rate decision, fresh inflation prints, and mounting election noise when you can let the macro dust settle? With Anthropic targeting a staggering $2 trillion valuation on the back of massive revenue acceleration, moving into October potentially gives institutional allocators a post-Fed clear view. For mega-caps, it’s likely not a retreat, just better execution. 

By the Numbers – IPO Filings and Offerings on Pace for Another Good Year

With 20 days still left in the third quarter, and all of Q4 remaining, new IPO filings as tracked by Wall Street Horizon are at 331 this year. By comparison, from Q1 – Q3 2025, new IPO filings only tallied 322, and that year ended up being the best for public debuts in four years. Currently we are on track to outpace that total if the macro backdrop can hold steady.

New IPO offerings, those that actually came to fruition, currently stand at 280 YTD, vs. 273 for Q1 – Q3 2025, demonstrating a similar pattern as filings. Again, if the growth landscape can hang in there and we don’t see any major impact from the looming geopolitical uncertainties listed above, we are on target for the strongest year for IPO offerings since the boom of 2021.

Are There Any Signs That Companies Are Getting Spooked?

So far we aren’t seeing much evidence of public debut jitters from private companies that set out the year with the intention to go public. Only ten companies that filed to IPO in 2026 have withdrawn those filings as compared to 18 from Q1 – Q3 2025, and 20 from Q1 – Q3 2026.

The Bottom Line

Don’t let September’s macro headline noise fool you. Today’s economic backdrop won’t likely trigger a broad market freeze like 2022, but there will be winners and losers. Cash-rich mega-caps, AI infrastructure plays, and scaled market leaders (the SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI tier) command their own gravity. For these names, sticky inflation and tariff chatter are just pricing variables, not deal-breakers. However, smaller, more speculative, and high-beta growth startups reliant on ultra-low discount rates are indeed taking cover until the Fed, commodity spikes, and midterm elections clear out. 

Portfolio managers are back at their desks, and the fall catalyst calendar is stacked. Keep your eyes on the October window, if Anthropic prices cleanly, it could encourage other names (ahem, OpenAI) to make their public debut by the end of the year.

data.title: AI Is Great at Generating Trading Ideas and Terrible at Knowing Which Ones Survive
data.description:
Ask a large language model or strategy generation software to design a trading strategy and it obliges instantly. Ask for fifty and it gives you fifty. They’ll look reasonable. Some will backtest beautifully. And that’s exactly where a lot of traders are about to lose money in a brand-new way.

The disconnect is simple once you see it. AI is genuinely good at one half of systematic trading and completely blind to the other half.

What AI does well: generate ideas

This is the language model and strategy generation software’s home turf:

  • It has read enormous amounts of trading literature and combines concepts fluently.
    • It never runs out of energy. Want twenty variations on a volatility-filtered mean-reversion setup? Done, faster than you could type them.
    • For a systematic trader, it collapses the tedious part of research, hand-coding variation after variation, into seconds.

That’s real value, and it isn’t going away.

What AI does badly: know which ideas are real

A language model has no built-in concept of out-of-sample validation. No walk-forward framework. No sense that testing 500 strategies and keeping the best means the best one is probably lucky.

It generates candidates. It does not vet them. And it hands you a gorgeous equity curve with identical confidence whether that curve reflects a durable edge or pure noise fit to the past.

Worse, this danger is bigger than it used to be:

  • The core trap in strategy development is the multiple comparisons problem: the more candidates you test on the same data, the more likely some look excellent by chance alone.
    • Test enough random rules and the best one always impresses you, edge or not.
    • AI and strategy generation software didn’t create this. It poured gasoline on it, because the whole point of these tools is testing far more candidates than you ever could before.

More candidates, more false positives, more beautiful backtests that die live, more blown accounts.

The fix: a two-stage pipeline

Don’t abandon AI generation. Stop treating a good backtest as a finish line and start treating it as an application to be reviewed.

Stage one: generate broadly.

  • Let AI do what it’s good at. Cast a wide net across different logic families, timeframes, and conditions.
    • Don’t fall in love with anything. A strategy here is a hypothesis, nothing more.

Stage two: validate ruthlessly.Vs Random Testing Create the best possible strategy by random signals, synthetic data. Let the best Vs Random strategy be your benchmark any real strategy must beat. If you cannot beat this benchmark, you may have found something by pure luck and no real edge.

Monte Carlo permutation testing scrambles the data to kill any real signal while keeping its shape, then runs your full selection process on the permutated data many times. If your real result doesn’t clearly beat that noise, the strategy is indistinguishable from luck.

The pairing works because it plays each tool to its strength:

  • AI supplies breadth.
    • Statistical validation supplies skepticism.
    • AI without validation is a false-positive factory. Validation without generation is slow and narrow. Together they’re the best of both worlds.

The mindset shift

The traders who will win with AI aren’t the ones generating the most strategies. They’re the ones who treat generation as cheap and validation as sacred.

Internalize the inversion: in the old world, the hard part was coming up with ideas. In the AI world, ideas are free, compute is cheap, and the hard part is disbelieving them.

Modern strategy-development platforms increasingly build this two-stage discipline in directly, automating both the broad AI-driven generation and the ruthless validation in one workflow, so the skepticism isn’t something you have to remember to apply.

However you assemble it, the principle is the same: let AI generate, then make every candidate survive a gauntlet before it ever sees real capital.

The idea is the easy part now. Proving it is the whole game. Everything can be automated now but you have to know what to automate!

David Bergstrom is founder of Build Alpha, a research platform for systematic traders focused on automatic strategy generation, strategy validation, portfolio construction, and market context. He can be reached at david@buildalpha.com or Buildalpha.com

data.title: Bargain Hunters, AI Bets, and CEO Confidence: Navigating the Final Wave of Q2 Earnings
data.description:
• Earnings slow down from this point forward, with only 737 global companies releasing results for Q2 this week
  • All eyes will be on the retail earnings (WMT, TGT, HD, LOW, TJX, ROST) and Nvidia results
  • Corporate uncertainty dipped back down in during the Q2 earnings season after spiking higher in Q1

From the Checkout Counter to the AI Trade: Key Earnings This Week​

American households are still spending, but with an intense focus on value. While the NRF projects a record $146.8 billion in back-to-class spending, consumers are heavily relying on early promotions and midsummer sales to stretch their budgets.1 

Solid retail sales figures confirm overall demand hasn’t stalled, but a cooling labor market and subdued University of Michigan consumer sentiment keep buyers selective. People are continuing to buy, but they are prioritizing essentials over discretionary items and favoring retailers with clear price advantages.​

This bargain-hunting environment sets up a stark divide for upcoming earnings. Walmart (WMT) remains uniquely positioned as its dominant grocery business continues to draw trade-down traffic from higher-income households, whereas Target (TGT) faces headwinds due to its heavier mix of discretionary home and apparel goods. High interest rates and a frozen housing market continue to delay large home improvement projects for Home Depot (HD) and Lowe’s (LOW), shifting focus to minor repairs and pro sales.

Meanwhile, off-price leaders TJX Companies (TJX) and Ross Stores (ROST) stand out as top beneficiaries as inflation-weary shoppers flock to discount channels for brand-name deals.​

Beyond big-box retail, the broader market narrative will hinge on Nvidia (NVDA), whose upcoming earnings reportserves as the ultimate litmus test for the mega-cap AI trade. Investors are closely scrutinizing whether massive hyperscaler capital expenditures are translating into sustainable enterprise returns or if the market is nearing a temporary digestion phase.

While tech sentiment has experienced intermittent volatility, marked by heightened skepticism around software monetize-ability and rising system costs, demand for hardware and infrastructure remains robust as next-gen chips roll out to cloud providers. Nvidia’s performance and forward guidance will carry outsized weight, determining whether the hardware-led AI rally can regain its explosive momentum or if Wall Street will press pause on valuation multiples.

Corporate Confidence Improves in Q2

The Late Earnings Report Index, our proprietary measure of CEO uncertainty, recorded a lower post-peak earnings season number in the second quarter after showing a slight but notable uptick in Q1 due to the instability brought by the Iran war.  

The LERI tracks outlier earnings date changes among publicly traded companies with market capitalizations of $250M and higher. The LERI has a baseline reading of 100, and anything above that indicates that companies are feeling uncertain about their current and short-term prospects. A LERI reading under 100 suggests that companies feel they have a pretty good handle on the near-term. 

The official post-peak season LERI reading for the Q2 earnings season (data collected in Q3) stands at 62, below the baseline reading. This suggests companies are once again feeling more certain about economic conditions than they were in Q2 2026 when the reading popped up to 73. As of August 12, there were 78 late outliers and 114 early outliers.

Q2 2026 Earnings Wave Wraps Up

In what is more-or-less the final big week of the Q2 earnings season, 737 companies are expected to release results (out of our universe of 11,000+ global names). Thus far, 73% of companies have reported.
